items.stem: Which is the word equation for photosynthesis?
items.answer: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
items.markingKey: Reactants carbon dioxide and water; products glucose and oxygen; light energy absorbed by chlorophyll.

items.stem: Explain why a plant is kept in the dark for 48 hours before one of its leaves is tested for starch.
items.answer: To destarch it: without light the plant cannot photosynthesise and uses up its stored starch, so any starch found later must have been made during the experiment.
items.markingKey: stored starch used up / destarched [1]; so starch found later was made during the experiment [1] [2]

items.stem: A variegated leaf has green and white areas. After testing with iodine, only the green areas turn blue-black. Explain this result.
items.answer: Only the green areas contain chlorophyll, so only they absorb light and photosynthesise, making glucose that is stored as starch.
items.markingKey: green areas have chlorophyll [1]; photosynthesis / starch only where chlorophyll is present [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas puts Canadian pondweed in a boiling tube of water and counts the oxygen bubbles given off in 5 minutes with a lamp at different distances (distance → number of bubbles): 5 cm → 43; 15 cm → 27; 25 cm → 19; 35 cm → 12; 45 cm → 7. Calculate the rate of bubble production, in bubbles per minute, with the lamp at 5 cm.
items.answer: 8.6 bubbles per minute
items.markingKey: rate = 43 ÷ 5 [1]; = 8.6 bubbles per minute [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena puts Cabomba pondweed in a boiling tube of water and counts the oxygen bubbles given off in 4 minutes with a lamp at different distances (distance → number of bubbles): 10 cm → 29; 25 cm → 20; 40 cm → 13; 55 cm → 8; 70 cm → 6. (a) Describe the pattern in the results. (b) Calculate the rate, in bubbles per minute, at 70 cm and at 10 cm.
items.answer: (a) The further away the lamp, the fewer bubbles are given off. (b) 1.5 and 7.25 bubbles per minute.
items.markingKey: (a) further away → fewer bubbles [1] (b) 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 [1]; 29 ÷ 4 = 7.25 bubbles per minute [1] [3]

items.stem: Lina puts Cabomba pondweed in a boiling tube of water and counts the oxygen bubbles given off in 4 minutes with a lamp at different distances (distance → number of bubbles): 5 cm → 41; 15 cm → 28; 25 cm → 33; 35 cm → 12; 45 cm → 9. (a) Identify the anomalous result. (b) Suggest one possible cause of this anomalous result. (c) Explain the overall pattern in terms of light energy.
items.answer: (a) 33 bubbles at 25 cm (more than at 15 cm). (b) Miscounting, bubbles of different sizes, or the plant not given time to adjust to the new light level. (c) Further away, less light reaches the leaves, so less light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and photosynthesis (oxygen production) is slower.
items.markingKey: (a) 33 at 25 cm [1] (b) any sensible cause [1] (c) less light / lower light intensity [1]; less energy absorbed, slower photosynthesis [1] [4]

items.stem: In a school laboratory in Auckland, a class adds sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water around some Canadian pondweed and counts bubbles for 4 minutes: 44 bubbles with a lamp at 20 cm and 31 bubbles with the lamp at 25 cm. (a) Calculate the rate of bubbling at 20 cm and at 25 cm, in bubbles per minute. (b) Suggest a more accurate way to measure the gas than counting bubbles, and explain why it is better.
items.answer: (a) 11 and 7.75 bubbles per minute (b) Collect the gas in a gas syringe or an inverted measuring cylinder and measure its volume, because bubbles may be different sizes.
items.markingKey: (a) 44 ÷ 4 = 11 [1]; 31 ÷ 4 = 7.75 [1] [2] (b) measure volume (syringe / cylinder) [1]; bubbles vary in size [1] [2]

items.stem: In a school laboratory in Lagos, a class adds sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water around some Cabomba pondweed and counts bubbles for 2 minutes: 40 bubbles with a lamp at 25 cm and 30 bubbles with the lamp at 30 cm. (a) Name the gas in the bubbles. (b) State the independent variable and the dependent variable. (c) Suggest why sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to the water.
items.answer: (a) Oxygen. (b) Independent: distance of the lamp (light intensity). Dependent: number of bubbles (rate of photosynthesis). (c) It releases carbon dioxide, so the plant does not run short of carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: (a) Oxygen [1] (b) independent: lamp distance / light intensity [1]; dependent: number of bubbles [1] [2] (c) supplies carbon dioxide [1]; so CO₂ is not in short supply / does not limit the rate [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis?
items.answer: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
items.markingKey: Six CO₂ and six H₂O give one glucose and six O₂; atoms balance on both sides.

items.stem: What is the function of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
options: It carries water up to the leaf
It absorbs carbon dioxide from the air
items.answer: It absorbs light energy
items.markingKey: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

items.stem: In a test, Ravi writes: "Plants get their food from the soil through their roots." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: Plants make their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis in the leaves; roots take in water and mineral ions, not food.
items.markingKey: food made by photosynthesis [1]; roots absorb water and minerals only [1] [2]

items.stem: Nadia puts Cabomba pondweed in a boiling tube of water and counts the oxygen bubbles given off in 4 minutes with a lamp at different distances (distance → number of bubbles): 15 cm → 30; 25 cm → 21; 35 cm → 14; 45 cm → 8; 55 cm → 7. Calculate the rate of bubble production, in bubbles per minute, with the lamp at 25 cm.
items.answer: 5.25 bubbles per minute
items.markingKey: rate = 21 ÷ 4 [1]; = 5.25 bubbles per minute [1] [2]

items.stem: Ana puts Cabomba pondweed in a boiling tube of water and counts the oxygen bubbles given off in 2 minutes with a lamp at different distances (distance → number of bubbles): 10 cm → 37; 20 cm → 23; 30 cm → 15; 40 cm → 9; 50 cm → 6. Calculate the rate of bubble production, in bubbles per minute, with the lamp at 30 cm.
items.answer: 7.5 bubbles per minute
items.markingKey: rate = 15 ÷ 2 [1]; = 7.5 bubbles per minute [1] [2]

items.stem: Lina investigates how light intensity affects photosynthesis in Cabomba pondweed. With a lamp 10 cm away, 64 bubbles are counted in 4 minutes; with the lamp 40 cm away, 8 bubbles are counted in 4 minutes. (a) Name the gas in the bubbles. (b) Name two variables that should be kept the same and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Oxygen. (b) Temperature of the water and the same piece of plant (or amount of carbon dioxide); so that only light intensity affects the rate (fair test).
items.markingKey: (a) Oxygen [1] (b) two control variables [1]; fair test reason [1] [2]

items.stem: In a school laboratory in Dhaka, a class adds sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water around some pondweed (Elodea) and counts bubbles for 4 minutes: 56 bubbles with a lamp at 20 cm and 40 bubbles with the lamp at 25 cm. (a) Explain why fewer bubbles are produced when the lamp is further away. (b) Suggest why sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to the water.
items.answer: (a) Lower light intensity reaches the plant, so less light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll; photosynthesis is slower and less oxygen is released. (b) It releases carbon dioxide, so the plant does not run short of carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: (a) lower light intensity [1]; less energy absorbed / slower photosynthesis [1]; less oxygen released [1] [3] (b) supplies carbon dioxide [1]; so CO₂ is not in short supply / does not limit the rate [1] [2]

items.stem: A greenhouse grower in Manila tests whether extra lighting is worthwhile. In a model experiment with Canadian pondweed, 56 bubbles are released in 3 minutes with a lamp at 10 cm, but only 30 bubbles with the lamp at 15 cm. (a) Calculate the rate of bubbling at 10 cm and at 15 cm, in bubbles per minute. (b) Explain why fewer bubbles are produced when the lamp is further away.
items.answer: (a) 18.7 and 10 bubbles per minute (b) Lower light intensity reaches the plant, so less light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll; photosynthesis is slower and less oxygen is released.
items.markingKey: (a) 56 ÷ 3 = 18.7 [1]; 30 ÷ 3 = 10 [1] [2] (b) lower light intensity [1]; less energy absorbed / slower photosynthesis [1]; less oxygen released [1] [3]

items.stem: Which mineral ion do plants need to make chlorophyll?
items.answer: Magnesium ions
items.markingKey: Magnesium is part of the chlorophyll molecule.

items.stem: Explain why a plant growing in soil that lacks magnesium grows slowly.
items.answer: It cannot make enough chlorophyll, so it absorbs less light, photosynthesises less and makes less glucose for growth.
items.markingKey: less chlorophyll [1]; less photosynthesis / glucose [1]; less energy and materials for growth [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why plants need nitrate ions even though they make their own glucose.
items.answer: Glucose contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; proteins also contain nitrogen, which the plant must absorb as nitrate ions.
items.markingKey: glucose has no nitrogen [1]; nitrogen from nitrate needed to make proteins [1] [2]

items.stem: Grace grows three groups of identical seedlings in different solutions for 30 days. Mean mass of a seedling (start → end): complete mineral solution: 2.5 g → 7.5 g; solution lacking nitrate: 2.5 g → 3.1 g; solution lacking magnesium: 2.5 g → 4.5 g. Calculate the percentage increase in mass for the seedlings in the solution lacking magnesium.

Tomás grows three groups of identical seedlings in different solutions for 30 days. Mean mass of a seedling (start → end): complete mineral solution: 3.2 g → 10.9 g; solution lacking nitrate: 3.2 g → 4.2 g; solution lacking magnesium: 3.2 g → 5.6 g. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in mass for the seedlings lacking nitrate. (b) Explain why these seedlings grew least.
items.answer: (a) 31.3% (b) Without nitrate the seedlings cannot make proteins, so they cannot make new cells and grow.
items.markingKey: (a) (4.2 − 3.2) ÷ 3.2 × 100 [1] = 31.3% [1] (b) nitrate needed for proteins / new cells [1] [3]

items.stem: Samuel grows tomato plants in water tanks in a greenhouse in Lagos. A concentrated mineral feed containing nitrate and magnesium ions is diluted at 2.5 cm³ per litre of water. (a) Explain why the nutrient solution must contain nitrate ions. (b) Suggest one advantage of growing crops this way in a crowded city.
items.answer: (a) Nitrate supplies nitrogen to make proteins needed for growth of new cells. (b) Mineral supply can be controlled exactly so growth is fast; needs little land (can be stacked or on rooftops) and uses less water.
items.markingKey: (a) nitrate → proteins [1]; needed for growth [1] [2] (b) valid advantage [1] with reason [1] [2]

items.stem: Farmers add fertilisers to their fields. Explain how this can increase crop yield.
items.answer: Fertilisers supply mineral ions such as nitrate and magnesium that may be in short supply, so crops can make more protein and chlorophyll and grow larger.
items.markingKey: fertiliser supplies mineral ions [1]; more protein / chlorophyll so more growth [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a plant wilts when it is short of water.
items.answer: Its cells lose water and are no longer firm, so they cannot hold up the leaves and stem.
items.markingKey: cells lose water / no longer firm [1]; support lost so plant droops [1] [2]

items.stem: Kwame claims: "Fertiliser is plant food." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. Fertiliser supplies mineral ions; plants make their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: fertiliser = mineral ions [1]; food made by photosynthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel grows three groups of identical seedlings in different solutions for 14 days. Mean mass of a seedling (start → end): complete mineral solution: 3 g → 9 g; solution lacking nitrate: 3 g → 3.6 g; solution lacking magnesium: 3 g → 4.8 g. Calculate the percentage increase in mass for the seedlings in the solution lacking magnesium.

A school in Lagos sets up a hydroponic tank of herbs. The label on the mineral feed reads: "Dilute 2.5 cm³ in each litre of water." (a) Calculate the volume of concentrated nutrient needed for a tank holding 80 litres of water. (b) Give two reasons why the plants also need water from the solution.
items.answer: (a) 200 cm³ (b) Water is a reactant in photosynthesis; it keeps cells firm for support (and carries mineral ions).
items.markingKey: (a) 2.5 × 80 [1] = 200 cm³ [1] [2] (b) any two reasons [1] each [2]

items.stem: A rooftop farm in Manila grows lettuces with their roots in a nutrient solution instead of soil (hydroponics). The instructions say to add 4 cm³ of concentrated nutrient to every litre of water. (a) Calculate the volume of concentrated nutrient needed for a tank holding 120 litres of water. (b) Suggest why air is bubbled through the solution around the roots. (c) Give two reasons why the plants also need water from the solution.
items.answer: (a) 480 cm³ (b) Root cells need oxygen for respiration, to release energy for absorbing mineral ions. (c) Water is a reactant in photosynthesis; it keeps cells firm for support (and carries mineral ions).
items.markingKey: (a) 4 × 120 [1] = 480 cm³ [1] [2] (b) oxygen for respiration [1]; energy for root cells / uptake [1] [2] (c) any two reasons [1] each [2]

items.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
items.answer: Photosynthesis
items.markingKey: Plants take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

items.stem: Explain how a carbon atom breathed out by a cow could end up in the cow’s muscles again.
items.answer: Grass absorbs the CO₂ in photosynthesis and makes glucose and other carbon compounds; the cow eats the grass and digests it; the carbon compounds are used to build muscle.
items.markingKey: photosynthesis by grass [1]; cow eats grass [1]; compounds used to build muscle [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why decomposers are important in the carbon cycle.
items.answer: They break down dead organisms and waste and respire, returning carbon to the air as CO₂ for plants to use again; otherwise carbon stays locked in dead material.
items.markingKey: break down dead material and respire [1]; return CO₂ for photosynthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists model the carbon flows in a grassland region each year (thousand tonnes of carbon): photosynthesis removes 180; respiration by plants and animals releases 72; decomposition releases 81; combustion of fuels releases 25. Calculate the net change in carbon in the atmosphere each year.
items.answer: −2 thousand tonnes (decreases)
items.markingKey: released = 72 + 81 + 25 = 178 [1]; net = 178 − 180 = −2 thousand tonnes [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists model the carbon flows in a grassland region each year (thousand tonnes of carbon): photosynthesis removes 200; respiration by plants and animals releases 90; decomposition releases 90; combustion of fuels releases 25. (a) Calculate the net change in atmospheric carbon each year. (b) State whether the carbon dioxide in the air increases or decreases, and name the process that is unbalancing the cycle.
items.answer: (a) 5 thousand tonnes (b) It increases; combustion of fuels adds extra carbon.
items.markingKey: (a) 205 − 200 [1] = 5 [1] (b) increases with combustion identified [1] [3]

items.stem: Mohammed uses hydrogencarbonate indicator, which is red at normal carbon dioxide levels, yellow when carbon dioxide increases and purple when carbon dioxide decreases. Each sealed tube contains indicator: tube A contains nothing (a control) in bright light; tube B contains a small water snail wrapped in foil (dark); tube C contains a piece of pondweed wrapped in foil (dark). The tubes are left for 4 hours. (a) Predict the colour of the indicator in tube B and explain your prediction. (b) Explain how this experiment models part of the carbon cycle.
items.answer: (a) Yellow: the snail respires, adding carbon dioxide. (b) Plants remove CO₂ from the surroundings by photosynthesis in light while all organisms return CO₂ by respiration, as happens in the atmosphere.
items.markingKey: (a) yellow [1]; reason [1] [2] (b) photosynthesis removes CO₂ [1]; respiration adds CO₂ [1] [2]

items.stem: Which organisms break down dead material and release carbon dioxide?
options: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi
items.answer: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi
items.markingKey: Decomposers feed on dead organisms and waste and respire, releasing CO₂.

items.stem: Explain why cutting down and burning large areas of forest increases the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
items.answer: Burning the wood releases CO₂ by combustion, and with fewer trees less CO₂ is removed by photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: combustion releases CO₂ [1]; less photosynthesis removing CO₂ [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the carbon dioxide concentration of the air stayed roughly constant for thousands of years before industry developed.
items.answer: Processes adding CO₂ (respiration, decomposition) were balanced by processes removing it (photosynthesis, dissolving in the oceans).
items.markingKey: adding processes named [1]; balanced by removal / photosynthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists model the carbon flows in a grassland region each year (thousand tonnes of carbon): photosynthesis removes 150; respiration by plants and animals releases 60; decomposition releases 52; combustion of fuels releases 25. What is the total carbon released into the atmosphere each year?
items.answer: 137 thousand tonnes

items.stem: Mei uses hydrogencarbonate indicator, which is red at normal carbon dioxide levels, yellow when carbon dioxide increases and purple when carbon dioxide decreases. Each sealed tube contains indicator: tube A contains a small water snail in bright light; tube B contains a piece of pondweed wrapped in foil (dark); tube C contains a small water snail wrapped in foil (dark). The tubes are left for 4 hours. (a) Predict the colour of the indicator in tube C and explain your prediction. (b) Name the process that adds carbon dioxide in every tube containing an organism.
items.answer: (a) Yellow: the snail respires, adding carbon dioxide. (b) Respiration.
items.markingKey: (a) yellow [1]; reason [1] [2] (b) Respiration [1]

items.stem: Which greenhouse gas is increased most by burning fossil fuels?
items.answer: Carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: Combustion of fossil fuels releases CO₂.

items.stem: Explain how greenhouse gases cause the Earth to be warmer than it would otherwise be.
items.answer: Sunlight warms the surface; the surface radiates infrared; greenhouse gases absorb some infrared and re-emit some back towards the Earth, so less energy escapes to space.
items.markingKey: surface emits infrared [1]; absorbed by greenhouse gases [1]; re-emitted back / less escapes [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why melting of ice on land causes sea levels to rise.
items.answer: Water from glaciers and ice sheets on land flows into the sea, adding to its volume (warmer sea water also expands).
items.markingKey: water added to oceans from land [1]; expansion of warmer water [1] [2]

items.stem: The table shows the mean concentration of carbon dioxide in the air measured at an observatory: 1960: 317 ppm, 1970: 326 ppm, 1980: 339 ppm, 1990: 354 ppm, 2000: 370 ppm, 2010: 390 ppm, 2020: 414 ppm. Calculate the mean increase per year between 1960 and 1980.
items.answer: 1.1 ppm per year
items.markingKey: 339 − 317 = 22 ppm [1]; ÷ 20 years = 1.1 ppm per year [1] [2]

items.stem: The table shows the mean concentration of carbon dioxide in the air measured at an observatory: 1960: 317 ppm, 1970: 326 ppm, 1980: 339 ppm, 1990: 354 ppm, 2000: 370 ppm, 2010: 390 ppm, 2020: 414 ppm. Calculate the percentage increase in carbon dioxide concentration from 1970 to 2000, and suggest one reason for the increase.
items.answer: 13.5%; more burning of fossil fuels (or deforestation).

items.stem: A transport company in Hanoi has 250 buses that each emit about 100 tonnes of CO₂ per year. Switching to electric buses is expected to reduce the fleet’s emissions by 60%. (a) Calculate the total carbon dioxide released by the diesel buses each year. (b) Suggest two other actions the city could take to reduce its contribution to climate change.
items.answer: (a) 25 000 tonnes (b) Any two: plant trees; encourage cycling and walking; use solar or wind power; insulate buildings; reduce waste.
items.markingKey: (a) 250 × 100 [1] = 25 000 tonnes [1] [2] (b) two valid actions [1] each [2]

items.stem: Which statement describes the greenhouse effect?
options: Ozone gas reflects sunlight back into space
Gases in the atmosphere let all thermal energy escape to space
Gases in the atmosphere trap some of the thermal energy radiated by the Earth
The atmosphere blocks all sunlight from reaching the ground
items.answer: Gases in the atmosphere trap some of the thermal energy radiated by the Earth
items.markingKey: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiated by the Earth and re-emit some back, keeping the Earth warmer.

items.stem: Explain how planting large numbers of trees can help to slow climate change.
items.answer: Trees remove carbon dioxide from the air by photosynthesis and store the carbon in wood, so less CO₂ remains to trap heat.
items.markingKey: photosynthesis removes CO₂ [1]; carbon stored / less greenhouse effect [1] [2]

items.stem: The council in Madrid runs 400 diesel buses, each releasing about 80 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. It plans to replace them with electric buses, which would cut these emissions by 40%. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide saved each year by the switch.
items.answer: 12 800 tonnes

items.stem: The council in Mumbai runs 500 diesel buses, each releasing about 80 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. It plans to replace them with electric buses, which would cut these emissions by 70%. (a) Calculate the total carbon dioxide released by the diesel buses each year. (b) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide saved each year by the switch.
items.answer: (a) 40 000 tonnes (b) 28 000 tonnes

items.stem: The table shows the mean concentration of carbon dioxide in the air measured at an observatory: 1960: 317 ppm, 1970: 326 ppm, 1980: 339 ppm, 1990: 354 ppm, 2000: 370 ppm, 2010: 390 ppm, 2020: 414 ppm. (a) Calculate the mean rate of increase from 1960 to 1990 and from 1990 to 2020. (b) Describe what these rates show. (c) Use the 2010–2020 rate to predict the concentration in 2030 and comment on how reliable this prediction is.
items.answer: (a) 1.23 ppm per year and 2 ppm per year (b) The concentration is rising and the rate of increase is getting faster. (c) 414 + 10 × 2.4 = 438 ppm; only an estimate, because the rate has been increasing and depends on future human actions.
items.markingKey: (a) 37 ÷ 30 = 1.23 [1]; 60 ÷ 30 = 2 [1] (b) rising [1]; rate increasing / accelerating [1] (c) 438 ppm with comment on reliability [1] [5]

items.stem: In which part of a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
items.answer: Chloroplast
items.markingKey: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are where photosynthesis happens.

items.stem: During a starch test the leaf is placed in hot ethanol. Explain why.
items.answer: Ethanol dissolves the chlorophyll and removes the green colour, so the colour change of the iodine can be seen clearly.
items.markingKey: removes chlorophyll [1]; so the iodine colour change is visible [1] [2]

items.stem: Felix claims: "Plants photosynthesise in the day and respire only at night." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. Plants respire all the time, day and night; in the light photosynthesis is usually faster than respiration, so the respiration is hidden.
items.markingKey: respiration continuous [1]; photosynthesis faster than respiration in light [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun puts Cabomba pondweed in a boiling tube of water and counts the oxygen bubbles given off in 2 minutes with a lamp at different distances (distance → number of bubbles): 10 cm → 60; 20 cm → 39; 30 cm → 25; 40 cm → 17; 50 cm → 11. Calculate the rate of bubble production, in bubbles per minute, with the lamp at 20 cm.
items.answer: 19.5 bubbles per minute
items.markingKey: rate = 39 ÷ 2 [1]; = 19.5 bubbles per minute [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia puts pondweed (Elodea) in a boiling tube of water and counts the oxygen bubbles given off in 4 minutes with a lamp at different distances (distance → number of bubbles): 5 cm → 43; 15 cm → 27; 25 cm → 18; 35 cm → 13; 45 cm → 7. Calculate the rate of bubble production, in bubbles per minute, with the lamp at 25 cm.
items.answer: 4.5 bubbles per minute
items.markingKey: rate = 18 ÷ 4 [1]; = 4.5 bubbles per minute [1] [2]

items.stem: A greenhouse grower in Manila tests whether extra lighting is worthwhile. In a model experiment with Canadian pondweed, 40 bubbles are released in 2 minutes with a lamp at 10 cm, but only 14 bubbles with the lamp at 20 cm. (a) Calculate the rate of bubbling at 10 cm and at 20 cm, in bubbles per minute. (b) Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
items.answer: (a) 20 and 7 bubbles per minute (b) 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
items.markingKey: (a) 40 ÷ 2 = 20 [1]; 14 ÷ 2 = 7 [1] [2] (b) correct formulae [1]; correctly balanced [1] [2]

items.stem: Which mineral ion do plants need to make proteins for growth?
items.answer: Nitrate ions
items.markingKey: Nitrate supplies the nitrogen needed to make proteins (amino acids) for new cells.

items.stem: Explain how root hair cells are adapted to absorb water and mineral ions.
items.answer: Each has a long, thin extension giving a large surface area in contact with soil water, and a thin wall so substances pass in easily.
items.markingKey: large surface area [1]; thin wall / close contact with soil water [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf grows three groups of identical seedlings in different solutions for 14 days. Mean mass of a seedling (start → end): complete mineral solution: 2.4 g → 6.7 g; solution lacking nitrate: 2.4 g → 3.4 g; solution lacking magnesium: 2.4 g → 3.8 g. Calculate the percentage increase in mass for the seedlings in the solution lacking magnesium.

A rooftop farm in Madrid grows lettuces with their roots in a nutrient solution instead of soil (hydroponics). The instructions say to add 2.5 cm³ of concentrated nutrient to every litre of water. (a) Calculate the volume of concentrated nutrient needed for a tank holding 250 litres of water. (b) Explain why the nutrient solution must contain nitrate ions.
items.answer: (a) 625 cm³ (b) Nitrate supplies nitrogen to make proteins needed for growth of new cells.
items.markingKey: (a) 2.5 × 250 [1] = 625 cm³ [1] [2] (b) nitrate → proteins [1]; needed for growth [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena grows tomato plants in water tanks in a greenhouse in Cape Town. A concentrated mineral feed containing nitrate and magnesium ions is diluted at 5 cm³ per litre of water. (a) Describe what would happen to the leaves if magnesium ions were left out, and explain why. (b) Suggest why air is bubbled through the solution around the roots.
items.answer: (a) Leaves would turn yellow because magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll; less photosynthesis so slower growth. (b) Root cells need oxygen for respiration, to release energy for absorbing mineral ions.
items.markingKey: (a) yellow leaves [1]; magnesium needed for chlorophyll [1]; less photosynthesis / growth [1] [3] (b) oxygen for respiration [1]; energy for root cells / uptake [1] [2]

items.stem: Name the process that moves carbon from the atmosphere to green plants?
items.answer: Photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: photosynthesis [1]

items.stem: Explain why the carbon in coal was not part of the carbon cycle for millions of years.
items.answer: The organisms were buried before they could decay (no decomposers / no oxygen), so their carbon was locked away until the coal is burned.
items.markingKey: buried without decomposition [1]; carbon stored until combustion [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists model the carbon flows in a tropical region each year (thousand tonnes of carbon): photosynthesis removes 180; respiration by plants and animals releases 81; decomposition releases 63; combustion of fuels releases 36. Calculate the net change in carbon in the atmosphere each year.
items.answer: 0 thousand tonnes (stays the same)
items.markingKey: released = 81 + 63 + 36 = 180 [1]; net = 180 − 180 = 0 thousand tonnes [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists model the carbon flows in a tropical region each year (thousand tonnes of carbon): photosynthesis removes 240; respiration by plants and animals releases 96; decomposition releases 108; combustion of fuels releases 40. (a) Calculate the net change in atmospheric carbon each year. (b) State whether the carbon dioxide in the air increases or decreases, and name the process that is unbalancing the cycle.
items.answer: (a) 4 thousand tonnes (b) It increases; combustion of fuels adds extra carbon.
items.markingKey: (a) 244 − 240 [1] = 4 [1] (b) increases with combustion identified [1] [3]

items.stem: Arjun uses hydrogencarbonate indicator, which is red at normal carbon dioxide levels, yellow when carbon dioxide increases and purple when carbon dioxide decreases. Each sealed tube contains indicator: tube A contains nothing (a control) in bright light; tube B contains a piece of pondweed wrapped in foil (dark); tube C contains a piece of pondweed in bright light. The tubes are left for 4 hours. (a) Predict the colour of the indicator in tube C and explain your prediction. (b) Explain why one tube should contain no organism. (c) Explain how this experiment models part of the carbon cycle.
items.answer: (a) Purple: photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so carbon dioxide is removed. (b) It is a control: it shows that any colour change is caused by the organisms and not by light or the indicator itself. (c) Plants remove CO₂ from the surroundings by photosynthesis in light while all organisms return CO₂ by respiration, as happens in the atmosphere.
items.markingKey: (a) purple [1]; reason [1] [2] (b) control [1]; shows change is due to organisms [1] [2] (c) photosynthesis removes CO₂ [1]; respiration adds CO₂ [1] [2]

items.stem: Suggest why scientists use temperature data from many places over many years, rather than one hot summer, as evidence of climate change.
items.answer: Weather varies from year to year and place to place; long-term averages from many places show the real trend and are more reliable.
items.markingKey: weather varies [1]; long-term / many places shows trend [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why burning biofuel made from crops grown each year adds less carbon dioxide overall than burning coal.
items.answer: The CO₂ released was taken in by the crops in photosynthesis only recently, so it is largely balanced; coal releases carbon locked away for millions of years.
items.markingKey: biofuel CO₂ recently absorbed [1]; coal adds stored carbon [1] [2]

items.stem: A transport company in Seoul has 400 buses that each emit about 100 tonnes of CO₂ per year. Switching to electric buses is expected to reduce the fleet’s emissions by 50%. Calculate the total carbon dioxide released by the diesel buses each year.
items.answer: 40 000 tonnes

items.stem: A transport company in Doha has 400 buses that each emit about 80 tonnes of CO₂ per year. Switching to electric buses is expected to reduce the fleet’s emissions by 70%. (a) Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide saved each year by the switch. (b) Suggest two other actions the city could take to reduce its contribution to climate change.
items.answer: (a) 22 400 tonnes (b) Any two: plant trees; encourage cycling and walking; use solar or wind power; insulate buildings; reduce waste.
items.markingKey: (a) 32 000 × 70/100 [1] = 22 400 tonnes [1] [2] (b) two valid actions [1] each [2]

items.stem: Which gas is given off by a plant photosynthesising in bright light?
items.answer: Oxygen
items.markingKey: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis and is released into the air or water.

items.stem: Explain why ethanol is heated in a water bath and not directly over a Bunsen flame.
items.answer: Ethanol is very flammable; a water bath heats it without a naked flame close to the ethanol.
items.markingKey: ethanol is flammable [1]; no naked flame in contact [1] [2]

items.stem: Mateo says: "Plants get their food from the soil through their roots." Explain why Mateo is wrong.
items.answer: Plants make their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis in the leaves; roots take in water and mineral ions, not food.
items.markingKey: food made by photosynthesis [1]; roots absorb water and minerals only [1] [2]

items.stem: Tariq puts Canadian pondweed in a boiling tube of water and counts the oxygen bubbles given off in 5 minutes with a lamp at different distances (distance → number of bubbles): 15 cm → 42; 25 cm → 28; 35 cm → 19; 45 cm → 13; 55 cm → 9. Calculate the rate of bubble production, in bubbles per minute, with the lamp at 35 cm.
items.answer: 3.8 bubbles per minute
items.markingKey: rate = 19 ÷ 5 [1]; = 3.8 bubbles per minute [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana puts Canadian pondweed in a boiling tube of water and counts the oxygen bubbles given off in 2 minutes with a lamp at different distances (distance → number of bubbles): 15 cm → 41; 25 cm → 26; 35 cm → 17; 45 cm → 12; 55 cm → 7. Calculate the rate of bubble production, in bubbles per minute, with the lamp at 25 cm.
items.answer: 13 bubbles per minute
items.markingKey: rate = 26 ÷ 2 [1]; = 13 bubbles per minute [1] [2]

items.stem: Isla investigates how light intensity affects photosynthesis in pondweed (Elodea). With a lamp 10 cm away, 64 bubbles are counted in 4 minutes; with the lamp 50 cm away, 6 bubbles are counted in 4 minutes. (a) Name two variables that should be kept the same and explain why. (b) Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
items.answer: (a) Temperature of the water and the same piece of plant (or amount of carbon dioxide); so that only light intensity affects the rate (fair test). (b) 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
items.markingKey: (a) two control variables [1]; fair test reason [1] [2] (b) correct formulae [1]; correctly balanced [1] [2]

items.stem: A plant grown without nitrate ions is most likely to show …
options: stunted growth and yellow older leaves
items.answer: stunted growth and yellow older leaves
items.markingKey: Little protein is made, so growth is poor; older leaves turn yellow.

items.stem: Suggest why growing the same crop in the same field every year can lead to yellow, stunted plants.
items.answer: Each crop removes the same mineral ions (such as nitrate and magnesium), so the soil becomes short of them unless fertiliser is added.
items.markingKey: same minerals removed every year [1]; soil becomes deficient [1] [2]

items.stem: Lina grows three groups of identical seedlings in different solutions for 30 days. Mean mass of a seedling (start → end): complete mineral solution: 3 g → 7.5 g; solution lacking nitrate: 3 g → 3.6 g; solution lacking magnesium: 3 g → 5.4 g. Calculate the percentage increase in mass for the seedlings in the complete mineral solution.

A school in Hanoi sets up a hydroponic tank of herbs. The label on the mineral feed reads: "Dilute 5 cm³ in each litre of water." (a) Calculate the volume of concentrated nutrient needed for a tank holding 250 litres of water. (b) Suggest one advantage of growing crops this way in a crowded city.
items.answer: (a) 1250 cm³ (b) Mineral supply can be controlled exactly so growth is fast; needs little land (can be stacked or on rooftops) and uses less water.
items.markingKey: (a) 5 × 250 [1] = 1250 cm³ [1] [2] (b) valid advantage [1] with reason [1] [2]

items.stem: A rooftop farm in Dubai grows lettuces with their roots in a nutrient solution instead of soil (hydroponics). The instructions say to add 10 cm³ of concentrated nutrient to every litre of water. (a) Describe what would happen to the leaves if magnesium ions were left out, and explain why. (b) Suggest why air is bubbled through the solution around the roots.
items.answer: (a) Leaves would turn yellow because magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll; less photosynthesis so slower growth. (b) Root cells need oxygen for respiration, to release energy for absorbing mineral ions.
items.markingKey: (a) yellow leaves [1]; magnesium needed for chlorophyll [1]; less photosynthesis / growth [1] [3] (b) oxygen for respiration [1]; energy for root cells / uptake [1] [2]

items.stem: In a carbon cycle diagram, an arrow goes from animals to the atmosphere. Name the process shown by this arrow.
items.answer: Respiration.
items.markingKey: respiration [1]

items.stem: Explain why there is more carbon dioxide in the air of a forest at night than in the middle of the day.
items.answer: At night there is no photosynthesis, but plants and animals still respire, so CO₂ builds up; in daylight photosynthesis removes it.
items.markingKey: no photosynthesis at night [1]; respiration continues adding CO₂ [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists model the carbon flows in a forested region each year (thousand tonnes of carbon): photosynthesis removes 120; respiration by plants and animals releases 54; decomposition releases 42; combustion of fuels releases 36. Calculate the net change in carbon in the atmosphere each year.
items.answer: +12 thousand tonnes (increases)
items.markingKey: released = 54 + 42 + 36 = 132 [1]; net = 132 − 120 = 12 thousand tonnes [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena uses hydrogencarbonate indicator, which is red at normal carbon dioxide levels, yellow when carbon dioxide increases and purple when carbon dioxide decreases. Each sealed tube contains indicator: tube A contains a small water snail in bright light; tube B contains a piece of pondweed wrapped in foil (dark); tube C contains a small water snail wrapped in foil (dark). The tubes are left for 4 hours. (a) Name the process that adds carbon dioxide in every tube containing an organism. (b) Explain how this experiment models part of the carbon cycle.
items.answer: (a) Respiration. (b) Plants remove CO₂ from the surroundings by photosynthesis in light while all organisms return CO₂ by respiration, as happens in the atmosphere.
items.markingKey: (a) Respiration [1] (b) photosynthesis removes CO₂ [1]; respiration adds CO₂ [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha uses hydrogencarbonate indicator, which is red at normal carbon dioxide levels, yellow when carbon dioxide increases and purple when carbon dioxide decreases. Each sealed tube contains indicator: tube A contains a small water snail wrapped in foil (dark); tube B contains a small water snail in bright light; tube C contains nothing (a control) in bright light. The tubes are left for 4 hours. (a) Predict the colour of the indicator in tube B and explain your prediction. (b) Predict the colour of the indicator in tube C and explain your prediction. (c) Explain why one tube should contain no organism.
items.answer: (a) Yellow: the snail respires and cannot photosynthesise, so carbon dioxide increases. (b) Red (no change): no organism, so carbon dioxide stays the same. (c) It is a control: it shows that any colour change is caused by the organisms and not by light or the indicator itself.
items.markingKey: (a) yellow [1]; reason [1] [2] (b) red (no change) [1]; reason [1] [2] (c) control [1]; shows change is due to organisms [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a rise in sea temperature can harm coral reefs.
items.answer: Warmer water stresses coral, causing it to lose the algae that feed it (bleaching), so the coral may die and habitats are lost.
items.markingKey: coral stressed / bleaching [1]; habitat / species loss [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana claims: "The greenhouse effect is always harmful, so we should remove all the carbon dioxide from the air." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. A natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life; the problem is the extra greenhouse gas from human activity (and plants need CO₂).
items.markingKey: natural greenhouse effect needed for life [1]; problem is enhanced effect [1] [2]

items.stem: A transport company in Colombo has 250 buses that each emit about 75 tonnes of CO₂ per year. Switching to electric buses is expected to reduce the fleet’s emissions by 50%. Explain how reducing carbon dioxide emissions helps to slow climate change.
items.answer: Less CO₂ in the atmosphere means less infrared is absorbed and re-emitted to Earth, so the enhanced greenhouse effect and warming are reduced.
items.markingKey: less greenhouse gas [1]; less infrared trapped / less warming [1] [2]

items.stem: A transport company in Toronto has 1200 buses that each emit about 100 tonnes of CO₂ per year. Switching to electric buses is expected to reduce the fleet’s emissions by 60%. (a) Calculate the total carbon dioxide released by the diesel buses each year. (b) Name one greenhouse gas other than carbon dioxide and give a source.
items.answer: (a) 120 000 tonnes (b) Methane, from cattle, rice fields or landfill (or water vapour / nitrous oxide).
